nameStory: The name 'Heart of Jesus' comes from the heart-shaped leaves that often display stunning patterns of white, pink, and red - colors traditionally associated with religious imagery of the Sacred Heart. The dramatic color combinations and intricate patterns on each leaf reminded people of artistic depictions of divine love, earning this tropical beauty its reverent common name.
description: Heart of Jesus is a striking tropical foliage plant grown as an annual in New England gardens. This showy plant reaches 15-35 inches tall and is prized for its large, heart-shaped leaves that come in dazzling combinations of white, pink, red, and green. Each leaf is like a living work of art, with intricate patterns, spots, and color blocks that make it impossible to miss in a garden bed or container.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large heart-shaped leaves 6-18 inches long with paper-thin texture and dramatic color patterns - typically white, pink, red, and green in various combinations of spots, veining, and solid blocks

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a compact clump 15-35 inches tall from underground tubers, with leaves emerging directly from the soil on long, succulent stems

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Leaf stems (petioles) are thick, juicy, and often colored to match the leaf patterns - feel smooth and slightly waxy to the touch

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Rarely flowers in cultivation, but when it does produces a small, inconspicuous white spathe (like a tiny peace lily flower) that's easily overlooked among the showy foliage

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Leaves feel thin and delicate, almost like colored tissue paper, and are easily damaged by wind or rough handling

habitat: Heart of Jesus is not native to New England and is only found as a cultivated ornamental plant in gardens, containers, and greenhouses. You'll spot it in shaded garden beds, decorative planters, and as houseplants, always in locations protected from direct sun and wind.

seasonality.spring: Planted outdoors after last frost as bedding plants or in containers, with tubers beginning to sprout their first colorful leaves.
seasonality.summer: Peak display season with full, lush foliage showing maximum color intensity in warm, humid conditions.
seasonality.fall: Leaves begin to decline as temperatures cool, often turning yellow or brown before the first frost kills the plant.
seasonality.winter: Not winter hardy in New England - exists only as houseplants indoors or as dormant tubers stored for next year's planting.

funFact: There are over 1,000 named varieties of Heart of Jesus, each with its own unique color pattern - that's more cultivars than there are species of birds in all of North America!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other 'elephant ear' plants like Colocasia or Alocasia, but Heart of Jesus leaves are much more colorful and delicate, while true elephant ears have solid green, thick, waxy leaves that can grow much larger.
contextualKnowledge: Heart of Jesus shares the common name 'elephant ear' with several other tropical plants in the same family, which can cause confusion at garden centers. The key is remembering that Heart of Jesus is the colorful, delicate one grown primarily for ornamental foliage patterns rather than dramatic size.
compareHints: Heart of Jesus is the only Caladium species commonly grown in New England. Compared to other Arum family members like Jack-in-the-pulpit or skunk cabbage, it's much more colorful and tropical-looking, lacks the distinctive hooded flower structure, and cannot survive New England winters outdoors.
